sources.title: TodoMVC behavior reference: precise functional contract

model.vision: A simple, dependable todo list that lets a small team capture, finish, and clear away their tasks.

objectives.statement: A team member can capture a new task in a single step, and correct or remove it later without re-entering it.
Users can mark any task, or their whole list at once, as done and reverse that decision just as easily.
Users can sweep away all finished tasks in one action so the list stays focused on remaining work.
Users can review their list as everything, only what remains, or only what is done, without the review ever changing their tasks.
Users always see, at a glance, exactly how many tasks they still have left to do.
No user loses their tasks between visits: the list they left is the list they find when they return.
The team's own agent tooling and shared workspaces can work the same todo list that people do, with the same results.
A small team can begin using the todo list for real work the day after it is delivered.

model.mission: Deliver the familiar, proven todo-list experience exactly as users already expect it, keeping every list on the team's own durable record rather than on the user's device. Offer that one list equally to people and to the team's agent tooling, so either can work it with identical results.

items.definition: A person on the team who keeps a todo list and works it day to day.
The team's own automated assistants that work the same todo list on a person's behalf, with the same results a person would get.
A team environment that hosts the todo list experience alongside the team's other embedded tools, so people can work their list without leaving it.
A single task on a list, described by its title and whether it is done.
The free-text wording that says what a todo is; a todo always has a non-blank title.
The ordered collection of todos belonging to one list owner, in the order they were captured.
A todo that is not yet done — still left to do.
A todo that has been marked done.
Add a new, not-yet-done todo with a given title to the end of the list.
Change the title of an existing todo without removing and re-adding it; revising to a blank title removes the todo instead.
Back out of a revision in progress, leaving the todo's original title untouched.
Take a single todo off the list regardless of whether it is done, leaving every other todo unchanged.
Record that a single todo is completed, without affecting any other todo.
Reverse a mark-done so a single todo is active again, without affecting any other todo.
In one action, mark every todo done — or, when every todo is already done, reopen them all.
In one action, remove every completed todo from the list while leaving active todos untouched.
The chosen way of reviewing the list — All, Active, or Completed; choosing a filter only changes what is shown, never any todo.
A review of every todo on the list, done or not.
A review of only the todos still left to do.
A review of only the todos already done.
The live count of active todos on the whole list, shown at a glance regardless of the review filter chosen.
A list owner coming back to the todo list after leaving or restarting; the list they find is exactly the list they left.
The team member (or the agent tooling acting for them) whose todo list is being worked.
Business activity: deciding whether offered wording is an acceptable title by trimming surrounding blank space and refusing wording that is blank.
Business activity: deciding what Toggle All should do — reopen everything only when every todo is already done, otherwise mark everything done.
Business activity: deciding which todos belong in the chosen review filter based solely on whether each is done.
Business activity: tallying the todos still left to do across the whole list, independent of any review filter.
Resource access: atomically add a newly captured todo to the end of the owner's list on the durable record.
Resource access: atomically replace one todo's title on the durable record.
Resource access: atomically take one todo off the owner's list on the durable record.
Resource access: atomically record one todo as done or not done on the durable record.
Resource access: atomically record every todo on the owner's list as done, or every one as not done, in one step.
Resource access: atomically remove every completed todo from the owner's list on the durable record in one step.
Resource access: retrieve the owner's whole list, in captured order with each todo's title and done state, from the durable record.
The team's own durable record of every list owner's todos, kept apart from any user's device so lists survive closing, reloading, or restarting.

items.name: Human interaction-surface volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: the surface a person works their list through. Today the same list is worked at the same time through an ordinary browser web app and through an MCP Apps surface embedded in the team's shared workspaces, alongside other MCP-hosted UIs (mission carry-forward 2). Different hosts give different capabilities, layouts, and interaction conventions. WHY volatile: the surfaces differ between users today, and the embedding host side is very young. MCP Apps and comparable embedding conventions have changed several times a year since they appeared, and that rate falls well inside this system's multi-year horizon (longevity grounding). LIKELIHOOD: high. A new or changed host is likely within the first year. EFFECT if not encapsulated: every host-specific way of capturing, revising, filtering, or showing items-left would leak into list behavior. A new host would then mean reworking the list rules, and the two surfaces would drift apart, breaking the mission promise that the experience is 'exactly as users already expect it'.

items.name: Programmatic access-protocol volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: the protocol callers use to reach the service. Today that is an ordinary web API plus an MCP surface 'so our other agent tooling can drive it too' (mission carry-forward 1, objective 7). WHY volatile: agent-tool protocols are changing fast. The MCP specification has had several breaking or additive revisions per year, and the team's agent tooling will keep adopting new transports and protocol versions. Historically that rate is many changes a year, inside the system's lifespan (longevity grounding). LIKELIHOOD: near-certain within 1–3 years. EFFECT if not encapsulated: protocol details such as framing, tool schemas, and versioning would bleed into the todo operations. Each protocol change would ripple into capture, revise, toggle, and clear behavior, and people and agents could stop getting identical results, which is the exact promise of objective 7.

items.name: Durable-record storage volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: the storage technology behind the Team Todo Record. Lists must live on the team's own durable record, not on a device, and must survive a service restart (mission; carry-forwards 3 and 4). The record also has to support the atomic list operations in the glossary: append, retitle, discard, set completion (one or all), purge completed, and recall in captured order. WHY volatile: 'the way we build everything else here' means storage follows the house's evolving standard, not something this product picks once. Team storage platforms (embedded store → managed database → house record service) typically change every 2–4 years, which falls inside this system's lifespan (longevity grounding). LIKELIHOOD: medium-high over 3 years. EFFECT if not encapsulated: storage specifics and their atomicity mechanisms would spread into every list operation and into the guarantee that the list is the same on every return visit. A storage migration would then touch the whole system and could put objective 6, no lost tasks, at risk.

items.name: List-ownership identity volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: how the system decides whose todo list is being worked. That means who the List Owner is, and how agent tooling acting for a person is recognised as that person. Today a list is scoped to 'a single user/session' (carry-forward 6). The glossary already says the List Owner may be a Team Member or the agent tooling acting for them. WHY volatile: a team trial that begins with session-scoped lists will be tied into the team's identity provider once real work depends on it (objective 8: 'start using it for real work'). How agents are delegated to act for a person (tokens, OAuth flows, workspace-granted identity) is also changing fast. Identity schemes for internal tools typically change every 1–3 years (longevity grounding). LIKELIHOOD: high within the first year of real use. EFFECT if not encapsulated: owner resolution would be wired into every operation and into the durable record's keys. A change from session to team identity, or a new delegation scheme for agents, would then force rework across every surface and could split one person's list into several.

items.name: Agent-delegation trust volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: what a caller is allowed to do to a list. A person at their own surface and an agent acting for them do not get the same trust today. Different agent tools and shared workspaces are granted different scopes at the same time. One may only recall and capture, while another may also clear completed or toggle all. WHY volatile: objective 7 requires agents to get the same results as people, but that promise holds only within what each delegation permits, and the team's agent tools have different permission levels side by side. Grant policies for agents are being revised quarterly across the industry as agent tooling matures, which falls inside the lifespan horizon (longevity grounding). LIKELIHOOD: medium-high as more agent tools are pointed at the list. EFFECT if not encapsulated: permission checks would be duplicated, slightly differently, in each access protocol and surface, and destructive one-step actions like Clear Completed and Toggle All would stay unguarded for some callers. A new agent tool would then mean auditing every operation.

rejected.name: Title vetting rule volatility
rejected.reason: Trimming surrounding blank space and refusing blank wording, including the rule that revising to a blank title removes the todo, is a closed, fully specified rule in the TodoMVC contract. A conditional handles it; it is not open-ended.

rejected.name: Toggle-all aggregate rule volatility
rejected.reason: The rule 'reopen all only when every todo is done, otherwise mark all done' is the TodoMVC reference behavior, and every implementation applies it the same way. The mission promises 'exactly as users already expect it', so changing this would mean changing the product itself.

rejected.name: Review filter set volatility
rejected.reason: All / Active / Completed is the fixed TodoMVC filter set, matched only on whether a todo is done. Every competitor offers the same three, and new filters would need todo attributes the contract rules out of scope.

rejected.name: Items-left counting volatility
rejected.reason: Counting the active todos on the whole list, regardless of filter, is a single well-defined tally with no open-ended variation. Code handles it with no architectural seam needed.

rejected.name: Todo attribute volatility (due dates, priorities, tags)
rejected.reason: The founder leaves the item's shape to us, but the contract explicitly says due dates, priorities, and tags/categories 'must not be assumed required'. Encapsulating richer todo attributes would be designing for a different product.

rejected.name: Multi-user list sharing volatility
rejected.reason: The contract explicitly rules multi-user sharing out of scope and scopes a list to a single owner. The real ownership change that is likely, session versus team identity, is kept as List-ownership identity volatility.

rejected.name: Manual reordering volatility
rejected.reason: Drag-to-reorder is explicitly out of scope. The list keeps captured order, which the durable record preserves without any ordering strategy.

rejected.name: Undo/redo history volatility
rejected.reason: Undo/redo is explicitly out of scope. Reopen Todo and Toggle All already give the 'reverse that decision' that objective 2 asks for, with no history mechanism.

rejected.name: Offline synchronisation volatility
rejected.reason: Offline sync is explicitly out of scope, and the mission deliberately keeps every list on the team's durable record rather than on the device.

rejected.name: Edit gesture volatility (double-click, Enter, blur, Escape)
rejected.reason: How a revision is started, committed, or abandoned is a surface-specific interaction convention. It is the same underlying change as Human interaction-surface volatility.

rejected.name: Frontend framework/rendering technology volatility
rejected.reason: The rendering technology for the web app and the MCP Apps surface changes with the surface itself. It is part of Human interaction-surface volatility, not a separate change.

rejected.name: Embedding host volatility (which shared workspace hosts the UI)
rejected.reason: Differences between shared-workspace hosts are exactly the cross-user variation that Human interaction-surface volatility captures.

rejected.name: Web API shape volatility
rejected.reason: The founder leaves the API shape to us. Its evolution is the same change as the move from MCP to future agent protocols, so it is folded into Programmatic access-protocol volatility.

rejected.name: Concurrent mutation consistency volatility (people and agents on one list)
rejected.reason: People and agents working one list at once is handled by the atomic resource-access operations in the glossary. How atomicity is achieved depends on the storage technology, so it is folded into Durable-record storage volatility.

rejected.name: Agent caller authentication volatility
rejected.reason: Authenticating the agent tooling is part of resolving who the caller acts for, which is List-ownership identity volatility. What the caller may then do is Agent-delegation trust volatility.

rejected.name: Hosting/deployment environment volatility
rejected.reason: 'Built the way we build everything else here' pins hosting to the house's existing platform, and no source suggests it varies or moves. Deployment choices belong to the operational concepts, not a volatility seam.

rejected.name: Cross-surface change propagation volatility
rejected.reason: Nothing in the brief or contract asks for live updates between surfaces. Recall on a return visit or reload meets objective 6, so a push and notification seam would be designing for a need no one has stated.

rejected.name: Completed-todo retention/archival volatility
rejected.reason: Clear Completed is defined as removing finished todos so the list stays focused (objective 3). No source asks to keep or report on cleared work.

rejected.name: Activity logging/reporting volatility
rejected.reason: This would be a reflex 'logging/reporting block' (siren song, ch. 2 §3.6) with no business ask behind it. The brief wants a simple, dependable list, not analytics.

rejected.name: Todo-list workflow volatility
rejected.reason: The sequence of list operations (capture, revise, remove, mark done, reopen, toggle all, clear completed) is the fixed TodoMVC contract, done identically everywhere. The volatility sits in who calls and where lists are kept, not in the workflow.

rejected.name: Scale/load volatility
rejected.reason: The product is for 'a small team to try out' and to use tomorrow. Designing for large-scale load has no grounding in the business ask.

rejected.name: UI localisation and pluralisation volatility
rejected.reason: Wording like 'item left' versus 'items left' and any later translation of labels is formatter-level variation handled by data or a conditional. It is not an architectural seam.

nodes.label: Request one change to the list (capture, revise, remove, mark done, reopen, toggle all, or clear completed) through the caller's surface or protocol
Resolve which list owner the caller is acting as
Check that the caller's delegation permits the requested change
Change permitted for this caller?
Vet the change against the list rules: trim and vet any title, settle what toggle all does, turn a blank revision into a removal
Does the vetted change alter the list?
Apply the change atomically to the owner's list on the Team Todo Record
Return the updated list with the recounted items left
Nothing changes: a blank capture, or a clear with nothing completed, is inert
Refuse the change as outside the caller's delegation

decisions.essenceRationale: Every customer of this product, whether a Team Member or a piece of Agent Tooling, buys one thing on the write side: the ability to change their own list and have that change be durable and identical no matter who or what asked. The seven customer-named verbs (capture, revise, remove, mark done, reopen, toggle all, clear completed) are permutations of this one abstraction; they differ only in which list rule vets them. The abstraction is nearly immutable. Every expected change (a new host surface, a new agent protocol, a storage migration, a move from session to team identity, a new delegation policy) sits behind a seam this flow crosses rather than inside the flow. What sets the product apart from a browser-memory TodoMVC demo is exactly this: one owner-resolved, permission-checked, atomic change to the team's own durable record, offered equally to people and agents. Volatilities crossed: interaction surface and access protocol (n2), list-ownership identity (n3), agent-delegation trust (n4/n5), durable-record storage (n8).

nodes.label: Ask to review the list under a chosen review filter (All, Active, or Completed) through the caller's surface or protocol
Resolve which list owner the caller is acting as
Check that the caller's delegation permits reading the list
Review permitted for this caller?
Recall the owner's whole list in captured order from the Team Todo Record
Match the todos that belong in the chosen review filter
Count the active todos across the whole list as items left
Return the matching todos with items left and the chosen filter
Refuse the review as outside the caller's delegation
The surface shows the result with the current filter indicated; no todo is changed by reviewing

decisions.essenceRationale: Every customer, person or agent, has to be able to trust what the list tells them: what is on it, how much is left, and that it is the same list they left. The three review filters, the items-left count, and the return visit are permutations of this one read abstraction. It is nearly immutable, because the TodoMVC filter set and count are fixed by the nature of the business. It is shared by every caller. And it is where the product's distinguishing promises can actually be seen: no lost tasks, identical results for people and agents, and one durable team record behind every surface and protocol. Without it the change side cannot be verified. Volatilities crossed: interaction surface and access protocol (n2), list-ownership identity (n3), agent-delegation trust (n4/n5), durable-record storage (n6).

nodes.label: Submit wording for a new todo
Vet the offered title: trim surrounding blank space and refuse blank wording
Title acceptable?
Append a new active todo with the title to the end of the owner's list on the Team Todo Record
No todo is created for blank wording

decisions.rejectionReason: A permutation of Change the Todo List in which the change is an append and the vetting rule is title vetting. It is ordinary list mechanics, not the essence of the business on its own.

nodes.label: Commit new wording for an existing todo
Vet the revised title: trim surrounding blank space and detect blank wording
Revised title blank?
Retitle the todo on the Team Todo Record
Discard the todo from the owner's list on the Team Todo Record instead of saving a blank title

decisions.rejectionReason: A permutation of Change the Todo List: a retitle, which a blank revision turns into a removal. It is the same owner-resolved, vetted, atomic change with a different list rule applied.

nodes.label: Back out of the revision in progress at the surface, restoring the original title on screen
No change reaches the Todo Service; the todo's title on the Team Todo Record is untouched

decisions.rejectionReason: The inert case of Change the Todo List: a change that is withdrawn before it is requested. The gesture belongs to the surface (folded into Human interaction-surface volatility), and the list itself never changes.

nodes.label: Ask to remove one todo, done or not
Discard that one todo from the owner's list on the Team Todo Record, leaving every other todo unchanged

decisions.rejectionReason: A permutation of Change the Todo List in which the change is a single discard with no vetting rule. It is CRUD mechanics, never core.

nodes.label: Ask to mark one todo done
Set that todo's completion to done on the Team Todo Record, leaving every other todo unchanged

decisions.rejectionReason: A permutation of Change the Todo List: a single-todo completion change. It differs from Reopen a Todo only in the value it sets.

nodes.label: Ask to reopen one completed todo
Set that todo's completion to not done on the Team Todo Record, leaving every other todo unchanged

decisions.rejectionReason: The inverse of Mark a Todo Done and the same permutation of Change the Todo List. It is a single-todo completion change with the opposite value.

nodes.label: Ask to toggle the whole list's completion in one action
Make the aggregate completion decision over the owner's current list
Is every todo already done?
Set every todo on the owner's list to not done in one atomic step on the Team Todo Record
Set every todo on the owner's list to done in one atomic step on the Team Todo Record

decisions.rejectionReason: A permutation of Change the Todo List in which the change is applied to the whole list and the aggregate completion decision vets it. The rule is fixed by the nature of the business, and the toggle is a convenience over mark done and reopen.

nodes.label: Ask to sweep away every completed todo in one action
Purge every completed todo from the owner's list in one atomic step on the Team Todo Record, leaving active todos untouched
With no completed todos the purge is inert

decisions.rejectionReason: A permutation of Change the Todo List: a bulk removal selected by done state. It is the same owner-resolved, permission-checked, atomic change to the record; only the selection differs.

useCase.name: Drive the List from Agent Tooling

nodes.label: Call a todo operation over the agent protocol on behalf of a person
Resolve the person the agent is acting for and check that the agent's delegation grants the operation
Operation granted to this agent?
Apply the operation to that person's list on the Team Todo Record with the same rules a person gets
Refuse the operation as outside the agent's delegation

decisions.rejectionReason: Not a separate behavior. It is Change the Todo List with Agent Tooling as the actor and an agent protocol as the access route. Objective 7 demands identical results, so the agent case must be the same use case; the protocol and delegation differences are volatilities, not new use cases.

nodes.label: Choose All, Active, or Completed as the review filter
Recall the owner's list from the Team Todo Record and match the todos to the chosen filter by done state
No todo's data or done state changes; the surface marks the chosen filter

decisions.rejectionReason: A permutation of Review the Todo List that differs only in which of the three fixed filters is chosen. The filter set is the nature of the business, not a separate behavior.

nodes.label: Look at how many todos are still left to do
Count the active todos across the owner's whole list, whatever filter is chosen

decisions.rejectionReason: A facet of every Review the Todo List result, and of every Change the Todo List result. Counting is a fixed tally (variableNotVolatile), not a behavior on its own.

nodes.label: Come back to the list after closing, reloading, or restarting
Resolve the returning caller to the same list owner as before
Recall that owner's whole list, with titles and done states, from the Team Todo Record

decisions.rejectionReason: Review the Todo List performed on a later visit. Persistence is a guarantee of the durable record that every core flow relies on, not a separate behavior; what changes between visits is identity and storage, and those are volatilities.

useCase.name: Work the List from a Shared Workspace

nodes.label: Open the embedded todo surface inside a shared workspace
Recall the owner's list from the Team Todo Record, exactly as the web app would show it
Changes made from the embedded surface follow Change the Todo List unchanged

decisions.rejectionReason: Not a new behavior. It is the two core use cases reached through a different host surface, and the host difference is captured by Human interaction-surface volatility. If the embedded surface needed its own use case, that seam would have failed.

verdicts.summary:
REVISE. One binding defect, under the actors-and-lanes rule. Everything else passes, and I approve the substance.

DEFECT (actionable). Swim-lane roleNames do not match the declared actors. Every use case declares actors "Team Member" and/or "Agent Tooling", yet the activity lanes use "List Owner", "Todo Service" and "Team Todo Record". None of these is a declared actor on any use case, and every node has linkedActorId = null. This affects both core flows (Change the Todo List, Review the Todo List) and every nonCore flow except "Drive the List from Agent Tooling", whose "Agent Tooling" lane does match. Fix: make every lane match a declared actor on its own use case. For example:
 (a) Declare "List Owner" as an actor. It is already a glossary term meaning the Team Member or Agent Tooling acting on its own list. Alternatively, keep Team Member and Agent Tooling as actors and set linkedActorId on the List Owner nodes so the lane maps to them explicitly. Objective 7 says people and agents get the same results, so one generalized List Owner lane fits the customer's reality. It only has to match.
 (b) Either declare "Todo Service" and "Team Todo Record" as system or secondary actors on each use case that uses those lanes, or rename the lanes to a declared actor. "Todo Service" is also not a glossary term. Use the system's glossary name, or add the term.
Change nothing else in the flows.

CHECKED AND ACCEPTED (do not change):
- Count: 2 core use cases, within the 2–6 range.
- Abstraction: 13 raw, customer-named use cases (capture, revise, abandon, remove, mark done, reopen, toggle all, clear completed, agent driving, filter, items left, return visit, shared workspace) collapse under two newly named abstractions. This is real subsumption, not a relabel.
- Rejection trail: every nonCore use case has a specific rejection reason, and every variationOf points at a core use case.
- Channels: "Drive the List from Agent Tooling" and "Work the List from a Shared Workspace" are rightly rejected as channel permutations covered by the surface and protocol volatilities. From the customer side this keeps Objective 7 intact: the same behavior, with the same results.
- Volatility exercise: all five staged volatilities are crossed by the core flows: surface and protocol (n2), identity (n3), delegation (n4/n5), storage (the n8 apply / n6 recall step).
- Essence rationales are substantive. They argue that the use cases are shared, nearly immutable and differentiating, which is what sets this apart from a browser-memory demo.

RESERVATION (taste only, not a revise reason): Change vs Review is close to a generic write/read split. I accept it because the rationales tie each one to mission objectives (1–3 for curating the list, 4–6 for trusting it). Objective 8 (usable for real work the day after delivery) and objective 6 (no lost tasks) both depend on the record being durable, so keep durability visible in the flows as it is now.
